claims.text: There are 3 ways an append draws a 429 in Nimbrel Ledger.

claims.text: An append draws a 429 when the `append` or `system_append` worker pools hold more batches than they have slots for.

claims.text: The command `nbctl pool status --all` reports worker pool status in Nimbrel Ledger.
claims.span: (`nbctl pool status --all`)

claims.text: An append draws a 429 when the ingest memory guard has refused the batch.
claims.span: The ingest memory guard has refused the batch (`nbctl guard report ingest --counters`).

claims.text: The command `nbctl guard report ingest --counters` reports ingest memory guard counters in Nimbrel Ledger.
claims.span: (`nbctl guard report ingest --counters`)

claims.text: An append draws a 429 when a circuit breaker has tripped.
claims.span: A circuit breaker has tripped (`nbctl breaker list --tripped`)

claims.text: The command `nbctl breaker list --tripped` lists tripped circuit breakers in Nimbrel Ledger.
claims.span: (`nbctl breaker list --tripped`)

claims.text: From release 4.6 and release 5.1 onward, appending to a `wide_text` column draws a 429 on its own account whenever the batch would otherwise have run the node out of memory.

claims.text: The workaround for Nimbrel Ledger 429 refusals is to take append and query load off the cluster for long enough that the queues drain and the nodes fall back under their limits.
claims.span: Take append and query load off the cluster for long enough that the queues drain and the nodes fall back under their limits.

claims.text: Where batches carry `wide_text` columns and the cluster runs release 4.6 or release 5.1 or later, the recommendation is to send fewer envelopes per batch.
claims.span: Where batches carry `wide_text` columns and the cluster runs release 4.6 or release 5.1 or later, send fewer envelopes per batch.

claims.text: A Nimbrel Ledger cluster that refuses appends has been given more work than its hardware can carry.
claims.span: A cluster that refuses appends has been given more work than its hardware can carry, so the answer is hardware: larger nodes (scale up), or more of them (scale out).

claims.text: The recommendation is to scale up first in most cases, and scale out when a further copy of the data for availability is wanted.
claims.span: Scale up first in most cases, and scale out when what is wanted is a further copy of the data for availability, per [the sizing notes](https://docs.nimbrel.example/ledger/sizing).

claims.span: Splitting a hot stream over more leader shards spreads append load across more nodes, which helps in some layouts.

claims.text: Where smaller batches do not clear the refusals, the next step is to add processor and memory capacity to the nodes.
claims.span: Where smaller batches do not clear it, add processor and memory capacity to the nodes.

claims.text: Raising the `ingest_guard.memory.leader.ceiling` cluster setting is the last step for `wide_text` column refusals.

A cluster that refuses appends has been given more work than its hardware can carry
so the answer is hardware: larger nodes (scale up), or more of them (scale out)

scale out when what is wanted is a further copy of the data for availability
